en: The Chanting of the Mantra from the *Zhongfeng Sanxi Jini Yanfan* (The Ritual Manual for the Three Times of Mindfulness), [Morning Session Complete; Dharma Master Circulates Incense;

Prostrations to the Buddha; Head of the Assembly Holds the Hand-Bell and Leads the Congregation in Circumambulation and Walking Meditation] Namo Amitābhayā-tathāgatāya-tathatāyāḥ. (1) Tathāgata. (2) Tathatāyāḥ. (3)
Yetha amili (4) dūpavi (5) amritā (6) sitambavi (7) amritā (8) vikalaṇḍe (9) amritā (10) vikalaṇḍa (11) gamini (12) gagana (13) jitakale (14) svāhā (15)
Cloud-Gathering Praise (The Assembly Stands Before the Buddha and Recites Aurally):
The West-Providing Assembly opens the gate to the Pure Land; Within the white radiance, we behold the Tathāgata. All Buddhas exclaim: "How marvelous!"
Forever liberated from the dust of the world, may we together aspire to ascend the lotus throne.
Clouds of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas gather;
[the Dharma Master ascends the seat and recites this verse:]
Five-colored clouds hang down; this is the seat of the Great Dharma King. Now that I ascend it once, divine beings and spirits shall protect me—may they always protect me, O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
General Outline (The Dharma Master, with dignified composure, visualizes Amitābha, performs prostrations, and recites with palms joined):
Three times of worshipful recitation of the inconceivable; The single path of perfect luminosity for the highest capacity.
Realizing the Dharma, realizing the mind, the mind is tranquil and illuminating; Formless and signless, transcending all marks.
The flowers of transgression wither and fall; the three miserable realms are stilled. The fragrance of the lotuses wafts upon the Seven Treasures Pond.
In every thought-moment, one clearly perceives the True Buddha. At this time, through awakening, one realizes Suchness.
Amitābha Tathāgata (Chorus): Bears witness to our focused mindfulness.
[The Dharma Master strikes the ruler once. Regarding the Dependent Origination:
I have heard that in the Western World lies the Pure Land, the Land of Bliss. The entire realm is adorned with a hundred jewels, and the various grounds are paved with the seven treasures.
The ponds flow with water of eight virtues, and lotuses emit four kinds of blossoms. Precious trees stand in layered rows, and auspicious light shines brilliantly.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha. In the past, during his causal stage, he made a vow:

"If there are sentient beings who call upon my name, they shall immediately be born in my land. For this reason, the three great bodhisattvas—Maitreya, Aśvaghoṣa, and Nāgārjuna—[composed treatises on him].

The ultimate aim of composing this treatise is as follows: tracing back through the successive generations of patriarchs, there are none who have not praised the Western Land and exhorted people to practice Buddha-recitation in order to transcend to the Ultimate Bliss.
This has continued down to my own time.

The Patriarch Zhongfeng composed the "Text on Binding the Mind. What is meant by "binding the mind"? It refers to binding one’s single mind exclusively to the Buddha, without allowing other thoughts to intermingle.
By relying upon this mindful mind, making it firm and fully cultivated, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

Now that I have the honor of presiding over this Dharma assembly, it is appropriate to offer incense and sprinkle pure water to reverently welcome the assembly of sages to descend like clouds; only then shall I expound the teaching for the multitude.
With equal devotion, extol the holy name and take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter: A-mi-t'o-fo | A-mi-t'o-fo | A-mi-t'o-fo | A-mi-t'o-fo | Mi-t'o-fo (The assembly chants in unison.

After the five-toned chant is completed, they rise again for another five-toned chant. Once the first four characters have been removed, the Dharma Master takes up the incense burner and offers incense.)
Incense Offering to the Great Dharma-Assembly for Opening and Establishing the Pure Land, Dedicated to Tathāgata Jvalanaprabharāja: First, we burn the incense of the Fivefold Dharma-body;
the sages of the Western Paradise gather like clouds. The arrayed saints descend their radiance to extensively proclaim and propagate [the Dharma].
This incense does not descend from heaven, nor does it grow from the earth. It is formed by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and flows forth from the ocean of true samādhi.
Forming clouds and mist, becoming canopies and pedestals, it nurtures the spiritual sprouts within oneself and yearns for the Awakened Father of the Land of Bliss.
Its name transcends that of Sukhāvatī, and its value outweighs that of Sahā. Incense it is; I burn it in the burner as an offering.
The Great Teacher of the Sahā World, the Most Honored One of Myriad Virtues, our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha;

and Amitābha Buddha, the Teacher of the Pure Land in the Western World and the Guide who leads us forth—may they assist and praise the West, transforming and delivering beings through their shared vows.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; the assembly of the Pure Ocean; those of the Three Worthies and Ten Stages; the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas;

from the Western Heaven and the Eastern Land; the various schools of Chan and Vinaya; all the patriarchs and monks; the deities and dragons who protect the teachings at the assemblies of the Vaipulya sutras; and the Great Emperor, Lord of the Stars.

The arrayed luminaries and sublime deities, the myriad spirits of the three realms, those of profound creation throughout the ten directions, the local deities of this mountain, and those who extensively protect this monastery—
along with the immeasurable sages and ordinary beings within this assembly for the Pure Land— may you all be universally permeated by these merits and together grant your compassionate descent.
The celestial wind wafts the incense smoke of red sandalwood; Auspicious mists and radiant light illuminate the great thousandfold world.
If you wish to know the place of peace and bliss of Nirvāṇa, Behold this single lotus blooming in the jeweled pond amidst fragrant clouds.
[Recite] "Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" three times. (At the conclusion, the Dharma Master takes up the water vessel.)
The Water Consecration (Holding the Twenty-Eight Exposed Kings Tathāgata’s Mantra to Consecrate the Water):
A single drop can purify the six sense-dusts; Wherever a drop falls from the tip of a hair, spring returns.
As one sprinkles the Dharma assembly, all becomes pure and clean; The multitude of sages from the Western Land all arrive like clouds.
Now, as for water: its original spring has a source; its function is to provide moisture and nourishment. It forms rain and drizzling showers, its grace universally soaking all things;
it becomes rivers and seas, its benefits universally saving all living beings. In the morning it submerges ten thousand li of mist and clouds;

in the evening it bathes the heavens with stars and constellations. Its ripples at the Xiang River and its surging waves at Yue Creek—Suxiu washed his ears therein in years past, precisely because of this.
How pure! In days of yore, the youth washed his collar and took its clarity; the receding waves gave rise to the sighs of the Sage of Kong;
and the overflowing basins inspired the metaphors of Mencius. Now, within the pool of the eight virtues, I have personally received it;
from the flask of the seven treasures, it has finally been divided and brought forth. Chanted with secret mantras, it is transformed into the water of Dharma.
(Recite the Great Compassion Mantra to sprinkle and purify, then recite the verse:
The Great Being’s supernatural powers are beyond description;
Seated upon a red lotus within the heart of the ocean, I pray that the water from the Bodhisattva’s branch May wash away the karmic enmity of all sentient beings.
Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Qingliangdi (three times).
Praise the World of Ultimate Bliss (the Dharma Master rings the bell and recites; after each praise, the assembly joins in song with the Buddha’s name):
The World of Ultimate Bliss is made of pure lapis lazuli; Rows of jewel trees stand in order in the four directions.
The ground is spread with golden sand and silver stairways; balustrades of jade and precious stones encircle it on all four sides.
I praise Amitābha Buddha, the Master of the Pure Land, whose name is Maitreya; by means of his forty-eight vows, he benefits the Sahā world.
May all nine grades of beings ascend to the other shore; I vow to deliver sentient beings from the river of craving.
Praise to the Body of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
Clad in pure white robes and wearing a flower crown, He seeks out voices to rescue those in suffering throughout the world.
The willow branch and pure water flask are both wondrous dharmas; Peacefully and serenely, they assist and support, displaying a compassionate countenance.
In praise of Bodhisattva Śrī-akṣobhya-vikrāmin:
Śrī-akṣobhya-vikrāmin is dignified and majestic, his virtue immeasurable; Six *liang* of robes hang upon him as he brushes away celestial fragrances.
Majestic is the place where he sits, its fragrance wafting afar; When he raises his feet and walks, he shakes the ten directions.
The ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas is boundless, Pervading the entirety of space; The radiance of the Dharma-realm leaves no trace behind.
With compassion, they welcome us back to the Pure Land; those with the karmic affinity will surely meet them directly.
We praise the multitude of sages and worthies of the Western Paradise;
having heard our invitation, may they all descend like clouds, and may the great assembly give rise to hearts of yearning and reverence.
I take refuge in the one praised for his compassion; with one voice we chant salutations to cultivate vast causes.
We praise the sages as they sit upon their seats;
their humble huts are transformed into expansive pavilions, and their chambers become vast and spacious with doors and windows wide open.
Thirty-two thousand lion thrones; upon each single flower pedestal, a Tathāgata ascends the precious throne, accompanied by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
[The Dharma Master strikes the ruler; the Head of the Assembly recites.]

The lay devotee [Name], who has steadfastly cultivated the Pure Land practice in [Province], [Prefecture], [County], and [District] of the Great Ming State in Jambudvīpa, together with the faithful [Names] and others assembled from the ten directions, wash their hands and burn incense to prostrate themselves before the Compassionate One’s countenance.
We, [Names], reflect deeply that the illusory retribution of this Jambudvīpa takes manifold sufferings as its cause; we have sunk into the mire of saṃsāra throughout vast kalpas, never once...
One must return to the source. How much more so when a hundred-year life exists but between a single inhalation and exhalation? The four elements are not of a permanent nature;

daily one is stained by worldly conditions and the body is entangled in the nets of the world. The mind-consciousness is constantly preoccupied with scheming and deliberation; how could its activities avoid transgressions and faults?
Thereupon, the delusion of delusions arises, and the karma of karmas is accomplished. Touching one's heart, one feels ashamed; reflecting upon oneself, one harbors remorse.
Relying on the Great Sage Śākyamuni, who opened the gate of skillful means and pointed toward the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss as the path for rebirth, [one proceeds] thereby.

This is to cast oneself in sincerity upon the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and to take refuge in True Suchness (*tathatā*). One lays bare all manner of sinful flaws and washes away every kind of karmic obstruction.

Respectfully hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* state that "even one who utters 'Namo Buddha' once has already attained the path of Buddhahood," and hearing Master Siji (Sishin) say, "If, by reciting Amitābha Buddha’s name, I do not attain birth in the Pure Land, may I fall into the hell of the plucked-out tongue."

In the Plow-Plowing Hell, I, [Name], venture to uphold sincerity and resolve, following my vows in practice. I have established a Western Paradise Assembly and cultivated the causes for the Pure Land.
Accordingly, I now respectfully convene at [Family Name’s Hermitage] a three-period *xiànniàn* (contemplative recollection) Pure Karma Dharma Hall.
Here, incense is burned, torches are lit, fruits are offered, and tea is presented; we read and recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Mahā-amitābha Sūtra*, and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

I shall expound upon the Mahāyāna Paramārtha-satya (the Ultimate Truth), the essential dharmas for the certain rebirth [in the Pure Land], the *Mida Daishaku* (The Great Prophecy of Amitābha), the *Jōdo Ganmon* (Vow Text for the Pure Land), as well as the invocation of the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) and the confession of transgressions and aspiration prayers.

Through the accumulation of these extraordinary merits, I pray exclusively that all of you may have no internal demons arise and no external obstacles produced; that your three karmas be as pure as ice and your six sense faculties as clear as snow, so that in this life you may achieve goodness.
The fruit is cultivated within the field of the eight consciousnesses; the sprouts of merit for others ripen within the pond of the nine lotuses.
May they universally repay the four debts of gratitude and equally sustain those in the three realms of existence. May all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm share this vow to be reborn there.
[The Master strikes the sounding-block to signal the chanting.
We have heard that the Teacher of the Western Land is the Guide who leads us across; his name is identical to that of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and his lifespan is said to be immeasurable.
His deep blue eyes clarify the four great oceans, and his white ūrṇā-hair curls gracefully like five Mount Sumerus. His benevolence is boundless, and his wondrous profundity is unfathomable.

There he beholds the transformation of the lapis lazuli gardens, with their pavements and steps adorned with agate. Within the jewel groves, he practices the Way throughout the six periods of the day;
within the golden ponds, the names of the nine grades are inscribed. Waterfowl and forest trees can preach the Dharma; the *kalaviṅka* birds discourse together on meditation.
The jeweled railings and jeweled nets cast shimmering reflections; the jeweled thrones and jeweled banners radiate brilliant light.

May the Buddha’s vows extend widely throughout the six realms and eight directions, compassionately delivering those in the three miserable paths. May he penetrate every atom to save sentient beings, achieving perfect interfusion everywhere to transcend all categories of existence.

He reveals the principle of non-empty true emptiness and opens the gate of wondrous existence that is yet non-existent. Thus he moves Avalokiteśvara to rescue suffering by responding to the sound of the cry for help.

We rely upon the power of Amitābha to deliver us through manifold means. We contemplate that for those such as ourselves, the roots of transgression are deep-seated and firm, while the veils of obstruction are heavy and pervasive.
We have bound afflictions into companions and stained by worldly conditions to form the seeds [of rebirth]. We do not awaken to the inner essence, yet we are entangled by external appearances.

Our attachment to profit and desire is profound, and our greed and voracity are expansive. Having forgotten the source—the treasury of awakening—it is difficult to hasten toward the Pure Land sanctuary. (The fourth assembly is gathered.)

The assembly, through diligent cultivation, offered prostrations and recitations throughout the three periods of the day. With ten thousand voices and diverse mouths, they chanted with a single resonance in a single thought-moment.
Setting aside their own inclinations to seek the source, they extolled the precious name.
(Sing the dharma of chanting the Buddha’s name. The leader raises the invocation;
the assembly chants in unison. Amituofo, Amituofo, Amituofo. Amituofo, Amituofo.
(When the five tones are completed, begin again with the five tones.)
Amitābha Buddha; Amitābha Buddha; Amitābha Buddha; Namo Amitābha Buddha; Amitābha Buddha.
First Period Buddhist Practice.
The Sutra of the Great Amitābha (Volume I) [or alternatively: The Smaller Amitābha Sutra] Recite the Mantra for Rebirth [three times].
General Outline: [Chant the Buddha’s name three times; strike the wooden fish three times; perform three bows.
The assembly sits in silence to listen to the lecture. For what reason is this world called "Ultimate Bliss"? It is simply because the various sufferings cannot invade it.
If a practitioner of the Way wishes to seek the path home, They need only recognize their own mind within the midst of dust.
Indeed, mind-mind is Buddha; clarified butter, cream, and curd are all produced from milk. Buddha-Buddha is but the mind; hairpins, bracelets, vases, and plates are all derived from gold.
A journey of a hundred thousand leagues does not separate east from west; Throughout the twelve hours of the day, ordinary beings and sages share the same path. One.
With palms joined, bowing the head once, the jade-green hair-tuft is as bright and radiant as the stars.

With one hymn of praise, with one song of eulogy, the golden-purple countenance roars like thunder and crashes like a storm; the moon of purity is embraced by every body of water, and the clouds of merit rest upon every mountain.

By invoking the auspicious name but once, one transcends the two deaths, crossing over like a fragrant elephant crossing a river. By raising the great name a second time, one puts all other birds to shame.
It is like the kalaviṅka bird emerging from its egg. When music is played, it moves through the dense trees; where waterfowl fly, lotus flowers abound—both the *puṇḍarīka* and the *utpala*.
At the break of dawn, they fill the lapels of one’s robes. White conch shells and red agates intermingle with the towers and pavilions of the springtime.
While the multitude of beings contemplate this as inconceivable, a single thought that turns the light back makes it easy to attain.
It has always been so; it ultimately does not abide outside the mind, but is clearly present right before one's eyes.

If this is truly so, then now, as you all focus your mindfulness on the vast and majestic name of Amitābha Buddha’s myriad virtues, let your practice during the three periods of the day be such that it does not involve deliberate cultivation toward realization.
Having personally received this single phrase of prediction, how can it be proclaimed?
The wind sighs through every tree in a thousand melodies; Fragrance permeates every pond with flowers of four colors.
(Recite: "The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden; he sits holding...")
Namo Amitābha Buddha (five hundred times; the Dharma Master strikes the ruler and raises it).
Namo Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the Ocean Assembly of Bodhisattvas (ten times each; when finished, chant):
Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Ocean Assembly (three times; pause briefly).
Lecture (The Dharma Master strikes the sounding block):
All sufferings arise from craving; Not knowing that craving arises from no cause, One forgets the self-nature of Amitābha Buddha.
Distracted thoughts racing in all directions are entirely Māra.
Remember the teaching of the Middle Way: arising yet without arising; the Dharma-nature is serene and still. Without arising, yet arising; karmic fruits remain manifest.
What is called "arising" refers to the traces of the birth and death of sentient beings. What is called "without arising" refers to the fundamental state of the nirvana of all Buddhas.
What is called "the serenity of the Dharma-nature" refers to the Dharma-nature inherently possessed by every person, which, though obscured by karma...
Ensnared by the net, they transmigrate through the five realms of existence from distant kalpas until the present life, falsely following the ascent and descent of birth and death.
One should know that birth arises from conditions, yet the dharma-nature does not arise together with those conditions;

cessation perishes from conditions, yet the dharma-nature does not perish together with those conditions. Therefore it is said that the dharma-nature is profoundly still (*zhanran*). This is what is meant by "profound stillness."
This is likened to water in an ancient well or a clear pool, where not a ripple stirs and not a breeze shakes it;
it is a single expanse of azure that mirrors the sky—this is what is meant by being "luminous, pure, and pristine.

It means that within the midst of the turbulent arising and ceasing of phenomena, the essence of the *dharmatā* remains profoundly still and unmoving. This is called "arising while being without arising. To speak of "non-arising while arising" means this.

Sentient beings enter the mind through delusion; accumulated karma results in fruit, and they undergo cyclic existence in vain, falsely perceiving birth and death—all of which are what is seen through the power of karmic fruit.
Upon the essence of the Dharma-nature, it is like a mirror reflecting images or a pearl changing with colors.

One should know that the light of the mirror is fundamentally pure and the substance of the pearl is free from blemish; yet, without contradicting the colors and images, objects and environments manifest one another. In reality, these are merely the mirror and the pearl.
It is fundamentally pure; thus one knows that the purity of the mirror-bead serves as a metaphor for our *dharmatā*.

The coming and going of those forms and images is like the manifestation of karmic fruits. This teaching clarifies that while Buddhas perceive only non-arising amidst the manifest process of arising and ceasing, sentient beings perceive only arising and ceasing within the profound stillness of non-arising. This is due to the presence of delusion and awakening.
They differ, and the measure by which they are perceived likewise differs accordingly. One should know that arising has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and non-arising also has no intrinsic nature.
Upon awakening, both arising and ceasing are non-arising; in delusion, non-arising is itself arising and ceasing.
Therefore, apart from arising and ceasing, there is no separate non-arising; apart from non-arising, there is no separate arising and ceasing. They are one essence with different names.
If this is truly so, then Amitābha Buddha is my own mind, and my own mind is Amitābha Buddha;

the Pure Land is this very realm, and this realm is the Pure Land. These differences arise solely from delusion and awakening; there is no gap between the sacred and the profane, nor between "this" and "that.
Thus, one knows that for the assembly before me and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, the day of birth [in the Pure Land] is certain.
It is certainly not arising; at the time of cessation, it is certainly not ceasing.

This very self-nature Amitābha, together with the tongue-faculties of the great assembly, universally and simultaneously turns the fundamental wheel of Dharma, unimpeded by any single thing. Do you all understand this thoroughly?
Listen further to a verse: [Verse omitted per instructions]
Arising and ceasing, non-arising and non-ceasing— In the Land of Bliss, who would dare forbid people from walking?
Who knows that within ten thousand fathoms of red dust, The lotus flower blooms at the first watch of the moon?
(The Dharma Master and the assembly descend from their seats; they move in the joy of the Dharma, circumambulating in the practice of the Way.)

Recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" five hundred times. (When the recitation is complete, the assembly returns to their positions; the Dharma Master, the Senior Monk, strikes the wooden fish once and raises it.
Recite "Namo Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the Ocean Assembly of Bodhisattvas" ten times each.
Namo to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pond Assembly (three times).
Repentance (the Dharma Master strikes the sounding block).
We have heard that within the fundamental nature of every person, Amitābha is inherently present; within the heart of each individual, there is entirely the Pure Land. To realize this...
Every step encounters the Buddha; those who attain sudden enlightenment find the Western Land at every stride.
(The Three-Period Recitation of Pure Deeds has now commenced. This concludes the first period of the ritual.

The assembly shall now recite the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Mantra for Rebirth*, and chant the sublime name of Amitābha Buddha’s myriad virtues one thousand times, followed by the invocation of the various sages.)

Each of these great names is recited twenty times. As for the aforementioned extraordinary merits, they are cast into the great ocean of Amitābha’s vows as virtuous causes and conditions, dedicated solely for the sake of [Name] and others, to eliminate past transgressions and to cleanse all grave and light offenses. Upon casting off this retribution body, [they shall...]

[May they] be reborn in the Pure Land. Furthermore, [I] contemplate that from time immemorial until this present life, following a single moment of delusion regarding the Truth, our six sense organs have pursued delusions as their foundation.
We have acted according to our own whims and committed non-virtues, creating karma in accordance with our passions.

As for physical transgressions, there were sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing; as for verbal faults, there was frivolous speech and lying; and in our deranged minds, greed and anger constantly arose, while false consciousness deepened.
Delusion and craving arise; through these three karmas, one becomes defiled by the six sense objects.
Thus, drifting aimlessly through the years and months, one is constantly entangled within oneself, perpetually mired in worldly toil without any thought of liberation.

Therefore, relying solely upon repentance and depending upon cultivation, I humbly pray that the transgressions of my eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind may be instantly eliminated at the mere thought [of this], and that [the defilements of] form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena...
The afflictions of the sense-object of touch are immediately purified and exhausted. One swiftly realizes the stage of *avaivartika* and accomplishes unsurpassed *bodhi*.
For the sake of [Name] and others, we now perform this sincere repentance. (The leader recites the verse while the assembly kneels and responds in unison.)
The first obstacle, the second speech, and the third poisons; The four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and the transgressions of the six sense organs;
The seven prohibitions and the eight difficulties are vast and boundless; The nine fetters and the ten entanglements—I repent them all.
With the preceding mind, clouds of sin arise to cover the sky; With the subsequent mind, the torch of merit extinguishes sin to shatter the darkness.
One must know that as a torch extinguishes darkness, it gives rise once more; throughout the six periods of day and night, one must diligently practice repentance.
Having completed the above repentance, one will not be entangled by the dust of worldly karma, and body and mind will be pure and white.

If one desires to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing and Ultimate Bliss, one must rely upon making vows; only then will one attain rebirth there. For if there is practice without vows, the practice...
One will surely be left in bewilderment. To have aspiration alone without practice is for that aspiration to be established in vain.

This day, the assembly, with one voice and in unison, focuses their mindfulness upon the name of the Ten Thousand Virtues of the Great Teacher of the Land of Bliss. His supreme conduct is manifest; if we do not make a vow, by what means shall we attain rebirth there?
With utmost sincerity, the assembly now makes this vow with a resolute heart.

Making the Vow (The Dharma Master visualizes the Four Noble Ones seated upright upon golden pedestals as witnesses to the vow; the leader of the assembly recites the verse while the congregation kneels and joins in):
May my illusory body be free from illness and suffering; May I escape the gates of the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties;
May all karmic obstacles from past lives be extinguished; May the afflictions and the six sense-faculties be eliminated.
May my body remain untainted by contact with the perverse and the wrong; May I emerge from the dust of the five turbidities of this Sahā world.
May I diligently cultivate practice without regression; May I enter the gate of liberation of the Tathāgata.
At the time of the end of my life, may my spirit not be disturbed; May the manifested Buddhas all come to welcome me.
May I reverently serve Amitābha and meet the assembly of sages; may I realize the indestructible diamond body.

Praise and harmoniously recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, the Unsurpassed King of Physicians. With his majestic golden countenance, he radiates light from between his brows; he acts as a vessel and a ferry across the sea of suffering.
The nine grades of the Lotus Land; may we all together aspire to go to the Western Paradise.
May this merit be universally extended to all, so that we and all sentient beings may together attain the Buddha-way.
The First Period of Buddha-Activities (Concluded).
The Ritual for the Buddha’s Memorial Feast:
The Sutra on the Repentance of the Thirty-five Buddhas (Next to be Recited).
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, eternally abiding;
Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions, eternally abiding;
Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions, eternally abiding.
Homage to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Homage to the various devas and bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma. (Recite three times.)
The "Universal Food" (wherein the Dharma Master holds a water vessel and pure food) is food created by the mind;
the entire food is the mind. Because essence and function are not distinct, one attains mastery over contraction and expansion.
Thus, the six sense objects mutually pervade one another, and the three virtues are eternally fused. Subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable, they give rise to the inexhaustible.

Relying upon the path of contemplation and secretly supported by the permeation of mantras, I shall lead [beings] toward virtuous ritual practices and cause them to perfectly accomplish the gift of Dharma.
Now, I uphold and recite this *Ananta-Tejas-Vaśitā-Prabhāsa-Parama-Viśuddha-Dhāraṇī*, and empower it.
Dharma-food. Cause it all to pervade (sprinkle it everywhere upon the Dharma feast).
The Mantra for Transforming Food: *Namo sarva-tathāgata-vajroṣṇīṣe*. Oṃ. Svabhāra svabhāra. Hūṃ.
(Recite three times) The Amṛta-mantra: Namo. Surūpāya tathāgatāya. Tadyathā. Oṃ. Suru suru. Phaṭ.
Raso lu. Pra-sa-lu. Svāhā (three times).

This food, with its color, fragrance, and flavor, is offered above to the Buddhas of the ten directions, presented in the middle to all the worthy sages and holy ones, and extended below to the various classes of the six realms of existence.

Bestowing equally without distinction, may all beings be fully satisfied according to their conditions. May this present donor attain the immeasurable *pāramitās*, the three virtues, and the six flavors.

Beings of the four modes of birth and six realms fill the sands of the Ganges; It is only because of a single initial thought that went astray.

With the bliss of dhyāna as fine nectar, you create offerings for the celestial kitchen. When you first attained the Way, the aged cowherd woman came forward to present her offering.

Preface (To be recited by the Head of the Assembly):

It is submitted that the Buddha’s vow to deliver sentient beings necessitates the steadfast practice of mindfulness of the Buddha. For anyone to realize sainthood, they must resolve to transcend the mundane world.
Bowing my head, I lay bare my foolish sincerity;
looking upward, I gaze upon the Great Awakened One. I reflect deeply that we, the multitude, have the honor of dwelling in Zhendan and the privilege of belonging to the human realm;
we are indebted for the compassion of the Triple Gem and rely upon it.

The fourfold kindnesses of creation—Heaven and Earth covering and supporting all, the sun and moon shining and presiding, the king providing the soil and water for birth and growth, and parents toiling with labor to nourish and raise us—we are unable to repay them. We are filled with trepidation and awe;

we are scorched and tormented within the vast fire-house of existence, and we are frequently defiled and attached by the dust of worldly toil. Though we harbor the intent to discipline ourselves, we lack the goodness to benefit others. This...

If one does not practice now, what will one rely upon in days to come? Sighing that time passes so swiftly, and grieving that birth and death are difficult to escape, one should abandon this Sahā world of the five turbidities and seek the pure land of the nine lotuses. First clarify where you shall fall;
truly, one cultivates the cause out of a longing for the fruit. Gradually treading the profound path, one proceeds from cause to fruit. Begin by gathering even a single drop of merit today.
On the auspicious day of the first day of the month (Jiazi), [I] established a Pure Land practice hall at the residence of [Name] Temple. Therein,
I burned the true incense of liberation and lit the wisdom-torch of radiant light,
chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha and offering praise.
Chanting the sublime names of the Bodhisattvas and reciting the golden scriptures, they empower the secret words of the Buddhas and fully prepare offerings for the feast.
Inviting both the holy and the mundane, they perform various meritorious deeds according to the ritual manuals, dedicating these toward the True Suchness of the Ultimate Reality.

They repay the kindness of their benefactors and provide sustenance to those with whom they have grievances, so that all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm may together perfect the All-Knowing Wisdom. [This is] the upper sacrifice.
Long live the Emperor! May the Crown Prince enjoy a thousand autumns! May all civil and military officials increase their rank and years of life!

May the winds and rains be harmonious, the state prosperous, and the people at peace! May every household be free from the anxiety of famine, and every family possess stores overflowing from their granaries!

Furthermore, we pray that for the patrons of this rite, the mountains of longevity may be layered with emerald green and the oceans of merit may swell with waves; may auspicious stars shine brightly upon their celestial mansions, and may auspicious vapors...

May your life-span be long and your destiny secure; may your household be harmonious and your gateways peaceful. May you remain healthy and at ease, with both old age and illusions subsiding. May there be benefit for both the public and the private spheres.
We pray that your faith be firm and steadfast, that external obstacles do not encroach, and that your aspiration for the Way be focused and single-minded, so that internal demons do not arise.

By the majestic radiance of the Buddha, may [the deceased] ascend directly to the highest grade.

We humbly pray that the Bodhi tree may grow ever taller, its shade sheltering hundreds of thousands of humans and devas; and that the *utpala* flower may bloom, its fragrance filling the great trichiliocosm.
May the noble families of our village and neighborhood all equally receive the grace of the Dharma rain;

may those who have passed away, according to their ancestral order, all attend the assembly at the Lotus Pond. Exhort your virtuous friends to encourage one another toward ultimate realization. May it be so!
The Buddha-Dharma has long endured and spread its influence. Throughout all four seasons, everyone relies entirely upon its comprehensive protection.
With profound reverence, we contemplate the Mind-Seal of the Buddha and offer this written memorial with focused mindfulness.
(Date: Year Month Day) A Memorial Petition Submitted for the Second Session of Buddhist Services:
The Great Amitābha Sūtra (Lower Volume) [or the Small Amitābha Sūtra as a substitute], accompanied by the Recitation of the Mantra for Rebirth (three times).
The Outline (Three invocations of the Buddha, three strikes of the ruler, three inquiries after the assembly’s well-being, and sitting in silence to listen to the lecture):
Having already attained Buddhahood this very morning, the Master who transforms beings in the Land of Bliss still deems it too slow;
how much more so for those who wish to go there? Take it for granted that their cycle of rebirth will never end.
Indeed, all throughout the ten directions is the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The mountain light and water colors are like space merging with space;

the entire earth is one’s own native land of pure peace. The blossoming flowers and singing birds are like mirrors reflecting mirrors. From this moment on, there is no returning; yet if one returns, one shall attain it.
"Who can vie with the misty scenery of the Five Lakes? His golden arms extend day and night; he permits only the man of the Way to entrust them.
His white jade whiskers have never been obscured throughout antiquity and today; we meet him now upon a narrow path. Therefore it is said:

'The myriad dharmas are the light of mind; all conditions are but the awakening of nature. Originally there is no one who attains enlightenment or anyone who is deluded; one simply requires realization this very day. Look before you, O assembly."
Fixing one’s mindfulness on the great name of ten thousand virtues: this is now the second period of Buddhist service. Let us first conclude with a single phrase.
How shall we proclaim it? (Strike the ruler; do not rise from one's seat.)
The bright moon shines upon the lapis lazuli ground; waterfowl sport amidst the blooming lotuses.
(Chant the Buddha’s name as before.
[The Dharma Master strikes the ruler.]
With Buddha in mind, one brings the mind to mindfulness; When mindfulness reaches the emptiness of mind, even the Buddha is forgotten.
Casting off all attachments, returning home, and examining once more— One recalls what was taught in the scriptures:
"Only mind. "Buddha is likewise only mind; sentient beings are likewise only Buddha. "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings..."
These three are without distinction; that which is called "mind-only" refers to the fact that the mind has many types.
There is the "fleshly heart," which is currently located within the five viscera and is produced from the blood and vital energy of one's parents.

There is the "discursive mind," which is that which presently gives rise to thoughts and discriminations regarding various objects, whether good or evil, favorable or adverse. There is the "conscious mind," which is...
It mingles with a thousand differences without becoming confused; it passes through the three periods of time without shifting. It shines forth, self-illuminating; it stands preeminent and alone.

It does not increase when in the state of a sage, nor does it decrease when among ordinary beings. Thus it is said: dwelling within the stream of birth and death, it is like a black pearl shining uniquely amidst the vast blue sea;
abiding upon the terrace of nirvana, it is like the crescent moon of the cinnamon tree shining solitary and bright in the azure sky—beyond all that can be grasped by form or image.
How could one distinguish between form and emptiness? The Sage realized this and provisionally designated it as "mind.
This mind cannot be known by wisdom (*jñāna*) nor cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). It universally contains all phenomena (*dharma*) while not establishing even a single speck of dust.

Because it universally contains all things, the aforementioned "fleshly heart" (*māṃsapiṇḍa-citta*) and the "discursive mind" (*ālambana-citta*) are both established based upon it. Is this true only for the single mind? No.

As for the encompassing and supporting of heaven and earth, the coming and going of cold and heat, the transformations and growth of insects, plants, and trees, and the manifestation of the dharma-realm as vast as dust motes—none of these appear except by depending upon it.
Because it does not stand [as a fixed entity], if one seeks this mind within all dharmas, it is utterly unobtainable. Although it is said to be unobtainable, yet within that non-...
Within the state of attainability, one is able to encompass all phenomena within the essence of the mind.

It is like rivers, streams, and mountain torrents returning to the ocean, all becoming water of a single flavor; or like jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets entering the furnace, merging into gold of a single color.

If all dharmas were to simultaneously lose their distinct names, this is what is meant by "not establishing [anything]. To investigate the origin of all Buddhas: they are the Buddhas of this very mind;
sentient beings, too, are the sentient beings of this very mind. Apart from the mind, there are no Buddhas; outside of the mind, there are no sentient beings.
Furthermore, although the names and characteristics of Buddhas and sentient beings differ in terms of superiority and inferiority, they all emerge [from the mind].

As for the fundamental source of one’s own mind, what distinction can there be between the sage and the ordinary person? Thus it is said: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Therefore, Yongjia said: "In a dream, the six realms are clearly present; upon awakening, all is empty, and not even a great chiliocosm exists.
One should know that to be deluded regarding this mind is what is called "dreaming," while to awaken to this mind is what is called "awakening."

It is said: this one Buddha and one Patriarch together extend their broad and long tongues and simultaneously emit pure sounds, elucidating the ultimate principle that "it is only mind, only Buddha, and only sentient beings. This is as clear as an ancient mirror and as precise as a scale;
when faced with it, beauty and ugliness cannot escape, and when used, weight and lightness are never concealed. Since this is so, one knows that the Western Pure Land...
The land: what is so extraordinary about this realm? The ancient Buddha Amitābha and this very mind are not different. Formerly, on Vulture Peak, [the Buddha] declared:
"Ten thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-lands to the west of here, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. The Buddha Amitābha currently resides there preaching the Dharma.
The sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings; they experience only various joys. Therefore, it is called 'Supreme Bliss' (*Sukhāvatī*). These words...
The Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) and Reward Land (Sambhogakṣetra) of Amitābha Buddha are not what is meant by the Dharma Body (Dharmakāya) Pure Land.
If one speaks of the Dharma Body, it is precisely this mind; if one speaks of the Pure Land, it is also precisely this mind. This mind is not here, nor is it there;
it does not cling to a location, yet it is not separate from a location. Because it does not cling to a location, how could it be outside of the hundred trillion lands? Because it...
Because they are free from spatial boundaries, the realms of dust, hair, and oceans of lands—throughout the four intermediate directions, above, and below—are entirely without obstruction.

Thus, there is not a single atom that is not a Buddha’s pure land. By this one may know that for the multitude before us, their birth occurs amidst lotus flowers blooming one by one, and their entry into death takes place beneath rows of jewel trees; there is not a single moment when they do not reach the pure lands. There is not a single...
Do not rely on a land of bliss for your mindfulness. Since this is so, tell me: apart from the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, is there any other place for deliberation?
To further explain this, I shall speak a verse.
Within the Great Perfect Mirror, all dust and defilement are absent; Amidst the azure lotus flowers lies the sacred embryo.
Gazing afar beyond the pools of golden sand, The precious light eternally illuminates the jade towers.
(Perform the ritual circumambulation and invocation of the Buddhas as before.)
Confession (The Dharma Master strikes the sounding-block):

We have heard that emptiness possesses resonance, like the sound of a valley; and stillness possesses formlessness, like the appearance of a Buddha. Although the sound of a valley arises spontaneously, it does not fail to answer when called upon.
The appearance of a Buddha, however, reaches the state of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*); it is not something to be struck for a response.
...yet they do not manifest. That which does manifest is like a toad ascending to the Milky Way, reaching over all things;

it is like the vast primordial waters surging through a great river, carrying all that flows along with them across. Truly, the marks of the Buddha are vast, perfectly pervasive, unimpeded, and inconceivable.
(The above was the establishment of the Three-Session Chanting for Pure Practice. Now, when...)
The second period of the Buddha’s work having been completed, the entire assembly shall recite the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Mantra for Rebirth*.

Each person shall individually recite the ten thousand virtuous and majestic names of Amitābha Buddha one thousand times, and invoke the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Ocean Assembly twenty times each.
By virtue of such extraordinary merit as described above, [one shall] be cast into the Great [Ocean of the Tathāgata].

May the merit produced within this ocean of vows be dedicated solely to the elimination of calamities and the extinction of transgressions for Gaō and others, so that upon casting off this retribution-body, they may proceed directly to the Pure Land.
Furthermore, I pray for [the deceased] and others: from beginningless time until this present life, like bubbles arising in a vast sea, our consciousness-waves have surged high and low;
like clouds dotting the great void, we have drifted hither and thither at the whim of the winds of emotion. Our eyes were deluded by forms and appearances, and our ears were confused by...

The sense-object of sound; the nose smelling various fragrances; the tongue tasting manifold flavors; and the body indulging in unwholesome tactile sensations—these constantly open the gates to all suffering.
The mind gives rise to frantic thoughts, perpetually defiling the realms of the six sense-objects. Thus, one cycles through the various destinies and revolves within the four modes of birth.
The ocean of karma is vast and boundless; the mountains of transgression are towering and steep. Were it not for relying upon confession and disclosure, how could they be dissolved and eliminated?

To expunge past faults and bring about future fruition, we again trouble the assembly of Dharma practitioners to sincerely repent. (The head of the assembly recites the verse, and the great assembly kneels in harmony.)
All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced by body, speech, and mind— I confess all these roots of sin.
Since sin arises from the mind, I shall confess with my mind; Having confessed my sins, how could they remain? Let the mind not arise again.
When sin perishes and the mind is extinguished, both are empty; this is what is called true repentance.
The preceding section on repentance is now complete. As for the subsequent practice, it is like a person endowed with eyes; may it be like the radiance of the sun, moon, and lamps.
Relying on the illumination of light, one sees clearly; only then can the practitioner reach the realm before them.

Therefore, if one recites the Buddha’s name all day long without making a vow to definitely attain rebirth there, then despite having the merit and practice of reciting the Buddha’s name, it will be rendered in vain.

This morning, the assembled multitude should join their voices in focused mindfulness, resolving to attain rebirth. Prostrating yourselves with utmost sincerity, you should now resolve your hearts to make this vow.
Vow. (The assembly leader recites the verse while the great assembly kneels in harmony:

May I swiftly know all dharmas; May I early obtain the eye of wisdom.

golden waves surge from the sea of suffering, and jeweled nets interlace, delivering sentient beings across the river of craving.

Outline: [The Dharma Master stands composed with palms joined, holding them level.

within boundless buddha-fields, may they be adorned with immeasurable fragrances, fulfilling the path of the bodhisattvas and accomplishing the causal origination of the Tathāgata’s fragrance.

I have heard that the Teacher of the Western Land, the Guide of the Nine Grades, has fulfilled his practices over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and perfected the merit of ten thousand virtues.
He manifested a golden body sixteen feet tall and extensively issued forty-eight great vows. His pores radiate the brilliance of white jade, and his complexion reveals the hue of pure gold.
In the West, he was formerly known as Amitābha; in the Eastern Land, he is now called Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus).
Guanyin assists him, and Shizhi follows in his train. His domain occupies the western quarter, and his land is named Sukhāvatī. On every side, the steps and paths are made of lapis lazuli;

in successive layers, the gates and railings are of gold and jade. Within the ponds of the seven treasures, the waters of the Dharma are profound, clear, and harmonious; upon the nine lotus pedestals, they bloom in profusion.
A celestial fragrance is sprayed abroad; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all give rise to joy. Water birds and forest trees proclaim the wondrous Dharma.

Among those in the world who can extol the Buddha’s name, this person is marked within the flowers. In a future life, they shall be born in the highest grade of the highest level, sharing the same name and title for eternal kalpas.
For those who recite and remember it, eighty trillion kalpas of sins are extinguished; for those who pay homage and offer praise, their merit is multiplied a hundred thousandfold.
In ten thousand ways, the merit is truly difficult to discuss; though praise may come to an end, our earnest entreaty remains. We pray that you will deign to grace us with your presence.
May the great assembly direct their sincerity and join in unison to offer worship and praise.

Incomparable and inconceivable, I now prostrate before it. The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so.

All phenomena are eternally abiding; therefore, I take refuge. Through the power of great wisdom and great vows, you universally deliver all sentient beings, Causing them to cast off bodies of feverish affliction and be born in that land of cool purity.
I now purify my three karmas, taking refuge and offering praise; May I, together with all sentient beings, [attain this].

Making the Vow (The Dharma Master strikes the sounding-block; the assembly kneels and recites):
I take refuge in the Teachers, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, Who proclaim the pure, subtle, and wondrous Dharma;
And in the Sangha of the Three Vehicles and Four Fruits who have attained liberation— I pray that you grant us compassion and graciously accept us.

I reflect that I have long contravened my true nature and entered pointlessly into the stream of delusion. Drifting and sinking with the cycle of birth and death, I have pursued forms and sounds with greedy attachment.
The ten entanglements and ten fetters have accumulated to form the causes of outflows; the six sense organs and six sense objects have falsely committed boundless transgressions.
Sunk in the sea of suffering and adrift on the path of heterodoxy, I have clung to self and indulged in others, misapplying the crooked and the straight throughout successive lifetimes.
Regarding my karmic obstructions and all transgressions, I look up to the Triple Gem with compassion and, with single-minded devotion, offer this confession and repentance.
I pray that the Muni may rescue and uplift me, and that virtuous friends may guide me, so that I may emerge from the deep abyss of affliction and reach the further shore of Bodhi.

In this life, may our foundations of merit, our lives, and our stations each flourish and prosper. In future births, may the seeds of wisdom and the sprouts of spirituality alike grow ever more luxuriant.

May we be born in a central land and always encounter enlightened teachers; may we leave the household life with right faith and enter the Path in our youth; and may our six sense faculties be keen and unimpeded.
The three karmas are pure and harmonious; they are untainted by worldly conditions. They constantly cultivate the Brahma-conduct and uphold the prohibitive precepts.

Mundane defilements do not invade them, and they strictly guard their dignified deportment. No harm is done to even the smallest crawling insects. They do not encounter the eight difficulties, nor are they deficient in the four conditions.
With the wisdom of *prajñā* before them, their bodhicitta never regresses. They practice the True Dharma and fully realize the Mahāyāna, opening the gates of the six perfections.
In the gate of practice, they traverse the ocean-like kalpas of the three *asaṃkhyeya* aeons; they erect the banner of the Dharma in every place and shatter the net of doubt in its many layers.
They subdue all demons and cause the Three Jewels to flourish; they serve the Buddhas of the ten directions without weariness.

They study and train in all dharma-gates, attaining complete mastery in each; they extensively cultivate merit and wisdom, universally benefiting beings as numerous as motes of dust. They attain the six kinds of...

Through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one perfects the fruit of Buddhahood within a single lifetime. Thereafter, without abandoning the *dharmadhātu*, one enters universally into the realms of worldly toil.

With a compassionate heart like that of Avalokiteśvara, one practices the ocean of vows of Samantabhadra. Whether in other directions or this world, one manifests a physical body according to the species and forms of beings to proclaim the sublime Dharma.
In the hells and the miserable destinies, or among the realm of hungry ghosts, one may emit great radiance, or...
Beholding these various miraculous transformations, all those who perceive my form, or even hear my name, shall give rise to the bodhicitta and forever escape the suffering of saṃsāra.
The lands of fiery cauldrons and icy rivers shall be transformed into fragrant groves; and those who drink molten copper and eat iron shall likewise be liberated.

They are reborn by transformation in the Pure Land. Those with fur and horns, those burdened by debt, and those harboring grievances—all their sorrows are brought to an end, and they all partake in benefit and joy.
In an age of pestilence, they appear as medicinal herbs to heal chronic ailments; in times of famine, they transform into rice and grain.

An Exposition on the True Cause of Buddha-Recitation:

I have heard that among the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Amitābha is foremost; among the Buddha-fields as many as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, Sukhāvatī is the ultimate refuge.

The ultimate principle is fundamentally nothing other than the mind itself, yet the initial gateway must necessarily proceed from the causal ground. Thus we know that even a tree of girth sufficient to encircle both arms...
A great tree begins from a mere hair-tip; a journey of a thousand li starts with the first step. Those who wish to transcend birth and death take the Pure Land as their destination;
those who seek to realize *nirvāṇa* find that mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is the essential means for rectifying the mind.
Deep faith in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the wondrous gateway to true liberation, and the contemplation of Amitābha is truly the compassionate father of all sentient beings. First, clarify this...
Since one must look toward the fruit in order to cultivate the cause, one gradually treads the profound path;

thus, by proceeding from cause to fruit, we know that there was a purposeful intent in gathering the multitude of sages to form a society (*shè*), and a deliberate teaching in encouraging others to focus exclusively on the recollection of the Buddha (*niàn fó*).

The cause encompasses the ocean of fruition; the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. When the form is straight, there is no shadow that is not upright; when the sound is harmonious, the resonance naturally accords.
Śāriputra demonstrated the essential method for attaining perfect penetration; the World-Honored One expounded the cause for cultivating pure karma: from hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
Ascending to samādhi and relying upon faith, practice, and vows, one enters the gateway of the Dharma-realm.

Thus, when a single thought arises, the myriad spirits take notice; when the mind of faith is born, all Buddhas appear. As soon as one invokes the precious name, one has already cast the seed within the lotus womb;

with a single aspiration for Bodhicitta, one’s name is inscribed upon the Golden Land. Those with the karmic affinity encounter this spontaneously, awakening and practicing on their own; yet those of shallow faith do not uphold it.
A great delusion and a great error! Therefore, it is said that the proclamation of the One Vehicle reaches the ultimate; in the end, one shall surely arrive at the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
When the myriad practices are perfected, the most supreme title alone is extolled as the "Precious Name. Grave offenses accumulated over eighty billion kalpas vanish like smoke in an instant;

distant realms spanning ten trillion kalpas are reached as swiftly as a feather’s flight. By focusing one's thoughts with single-minded devotion, one perceives the Buddha through the very contemplation of the mind.

Body and mind intersect; thus, through the gateway of causes, one achieves the supreme fruit. The pure and impure lands of the ten directions—whether contracted or expanded—are simultaneously contained within the tip of a single hair.
A single nature encompasses and harmonizes them, vast and expansive, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

In this way, Buddhas and sentient beings penetrate one another; pure lands and defiled lands communicate in profound stillness. Each contains the other; phenomena and principle are unimpeded, like a spirit.
A single jewel suddenly contains all manner of treasures, just as the celestial net reflects a thousand intermingling lights. Since my own mind is thus, the Buddhas of the past are likewise so.

Postscript to the Re-engraving of the *Sāmayika-smaraṇa* (Recollection of the Three Times):

I observe that among the common people of the world, whenever they seek blessings, avert calamities, prolong life, or escort the deceased, they often place their faith in the heterodox teachings of shamans and sorcerers.
Some slaughter livestock to summon malevolent spirits (*māra*), while others gather in crowds to propagate the Luo teachings. As for the scholar-gentry...
Among the families of high officials, there are likewise many who follow these [erroneous views] without awakening; I deeply lament this.

Now, between these two—one is the taking of life, and the other is the recitation of the Buddha’s name—how could they not be worlds apart? Yet, in the final analysis, both result in entry into hell as swiftly as an arrow.

Why is this? They slaughter living beings in pursuit of blessings, yet they compare this to killing humans to curry favor with others. Before they have received any blessing, their transgressions instead increase;
as life and death repay one another, there will be no end to their days in hell—how tragic! This is especially severe among those in the world who follow the Luo Teaching (Luoism).
For the most part, they mouth the name of the Bodhisattva while practicing the conduct of an icchantika; they are most convenient for being like owls.
Those who are obstinate, wicked, and sycophantic rely upon this [excuse] to satisfy their desires and indulge their own whims, reaching points that are truly不忍言 (unbearable to speak of).
Furthermore, the prohibition against sexual misconduct is the foremost principle of the Buddha; yet they consider it to be harmless. As for funeral rites and sacrifices—

This is the foremost concern for those born as human beings. Yet they eliminate it entirely and pay no heed to it. Foolish men and women follow their teachings, considering them extremely convenient and effortless;
moreover, they rely upon them to greedily consume offerings of faith, regarding this as a great profit free from suffering.
Thus they lead one another into hell, and there is still no end in sight—how much more so!
How lamentable! Alas, alas! Worldly people give rise to existence through craving and yet place their faith in heterodox sorcerers, ultimately performing deeds that lead to the extinction of life.
They follow the Buddha and yet place their faith in heterodox teachers, ultimately performing deeds that constitute slandering the Buddha. How aimless they are!
It is like traveling at night without a torch, or crossing a great river without a boat or oars. How tragic, how tragic! I have humbly observed this...
